content: Acacia mellifera is a perennial tree that is not currently classified as a threatened species. The species name mellifera is derived from its sweet-smelling blossoms and its association with honey. The wood of this tree turns a deep pitch black when treated with oil. It is commonly referred to as Blackthorn or Swaarthaak in Afrikaans. Distribution Acacia mellifera is native to and predominantly found in arid regions of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, Australia, India, and areas surrounding the Indian Ocean. Characteristics This species can grow either as a multi-trunked shrub, reaching heights of up to seven meters, with a crown that is generally funnel-shaped, or as a small single-trunked tree that can grow up to nine meters tall. Acacia mellifera reproduces both through seed formation and vegetative propagation via stick excursions, which can result in the formation of dense, impenetrable thickets comprising hundreds of individual plants. Uses In the dry regions of Africa, Acacia mellifera serves multiple purposes. It is utilized as fencing material, livestock feed, and as a building material for constructing huts. In some areas, the nectar from its blossoms is consumed as food. Medicinally, the milky sap of the tree is used to induce vomiting, while the boiled bark is employed in the treatment of abdominal pain, pneumonia, and malaria. Animal Uses This tree is a vital source of nutrition for both domesticated livestock and wild animals, particularly in the arid regions of Africa. Its leaves and young branches are highly nutritious, containing a significant amount of protein. The flowers are frequently consumed by kudu, while common browsers of the tree include black rhinoceroses, giraffes, and elands.
